newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea seeks to shore up confidence in banks.
newsitem.headline: South Korea seeks to shore up confidence in banks.

text.p: South Korea's finance minister, seeking to shore up confidence in the financial system following two major corporate failures, on Tuesday pledged help for banks suffering a liquidity crunch.
Kang Kyong-shik also promised to assist banks having trouble raising funds overseas.
In a speech to the nation's top bankers, Kang said authorities would take steps to "prevent a series of recent incidents from damaging external credibility and the stability of the banking system".

His comments came a day after the central Bank of Korea announced it would extend $1 billion in short-term financing to banks whose overseas borrowing costs have shot up since the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January.
The borrowing crunch, made worse after Sammi Steel Co foundered this month, has pushed up local interest rates and sparked fears that other heavily-indebted companies could also sink.
The president of Korea First Bank, the prime lender to both steelmakers, on Monday denied rumours of a run on the bank.
"The government will actively take necessary steps if individual financial institutions face difficulties in their funding operations," Kang said, without elaborating.
An aide to Kang said the minister was referring to banks suffering a short-term liquidity crunch.
"The government will assist local banks facing difficulties borrowing money from abroad," Kang said.
The aide explained the government planned to use its foreign currency holdings to lend to domestic institutions and cover the lending with overseas borrowing through state-run banks.
Separately, President Kim Young-sam ordered his cabinet to take steps to stabilise financial markets hit hard by the twin corporate meltdowns.

"The government should do its best to stabilise money and foreign exchange markets troubled by the application for court receivership by Sammi companies that followed the Hanbo incident," he told a cabinet meeting.
Banks have been paying a higher "Korea premium" on overseas loans since Hanbo Steel failed under $5.8 billion of debt.
Some are paying 45-50 basis points above the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) for one- to six-month term deposits. Before the the Hanbo collapse,the premium was 25-30 bais points above LIBOR.
On Monday, the Bank of Korea said it would supply a total of $1 billion to seven local banks this month to help ease the dollar shortage.
It was the second time since Hanbo's collapse that the central bank has offered to inject $1 billion. The previous occasion was on February 7.

Newspapers on Tuesday, quoting an unnamed central bank official, said the latest $1 billion included $300 million for Korea First Bank, the main creditor to both failed steelmakers, and $150 million each for Cho Hung Bank, Commercial Bank of Korea and SEOULBANK
A dollar shortage is pushing the domestic currency to new lows. The won sagged again on Tuesday, ending at its weakest close in seven years at 888.70 to the dollar after opening at 888.20.
